subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments
title: Arjun's First Digital Payment
hook: A boy learns how money travels invisibly through phones and computers.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A Class 7 student who gets his first pocket money and smartphone

characters.name: Mom
characters.role: Teaches Arjun about safe digital money

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: A fintech teacher who explains UPI and cards

image.alt: Arjun's First Digital Payment — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Money Without Paper
slides.storyContext: Arjun gets ₹500 pocket money from his parents. His mom says, 'Instead of cash, let's open a digital wallet and UPI account on your phone. You can spend without coins!' Arjun is amazed: 'How? Where does the money go?'

image.alt: Money Without Paper — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: What Is Digital Money?
slides.storyContext: Ravi explains in class: 'Digital money is NOT fake money. It's REAL money (rupees) that lives inside your phone or bank account instead of your pocket. When you send digital money, it travels through internet wires to the other person's account. Banks track everything.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Digital money is real rupees stored in your bank or digital wallet, sent through the internet.

points.label: How it works
points.text: Your bank account = a vault. Digital wallet = a smaller pouch. Both hold real money.

slides.inSimpleWords: It's like your money traveled from your bank to their bank through magic wires, but banks know every rupee that moved.

image.alt: What Is Digital Money? — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: UPI — Unified Payments Interface
slides.storyContext: Mom downloads Google Pay on Arjun's phone and links his bank account. 'This is UPI,' she says. 'You give a unique ID (like arjun@upi) and people can send you money instantly. You can also send to friends by their UPI ID.'

points.label: What is UPI
points.text: A system that lets you send and receive money using just a phone number or ID.

points.label: UPI ID (VPA)
points.text: Your identity: arjun@upi or arjun@googleplay (the @upi part is the bank provider).

points.label: Speed
points.text: UPI is INSTANT — money reaches in seconds, 24/7, even on holidays.

slides.inSimpleWords: UPI is the fastest way to send money between friends. It's like giving someone your bank address; they deposit directly.

image.alt: UPI — Unified Payments Interface — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: How to Use UPI — Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Arjun's friend Zara asks him to pay her ₹100 for a shared snack. Arjun opens Google Pay and follows these steps Mom taught him.

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Open your UPI app (Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, etc.)

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Click 'Send Money' and enter the receiver's UPI ID.

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Type the amount (₹100) and tap 'Send'.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Enter your PIN (like a password) to confirm.

points.label: Step 5
points.text: Done! Money reaches Zara instantly. You get a receipt.

slides.inSimpleWords: UPI is easier than handing cash—no coins, no change, no loss.

image.alt: How to Use UPI — Step by Step — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Debit Cards — Your Bank in Your Pocket
slides.storyContext: At the ice cream shop, Arjun sees his dad use a card to pay. Dad says: 'This is a debit card. It's directly linked to my bank account. When I swipe it, money comes from my account instantly, just like UPI.'

points.label: What is a debit card
points.text: A plastic card linked to your bank account. Spend only what's in your account.

points.label: How it works
points.text: You swipe/insert/tap the card. The shop connects to your bank. Your account is debited (money is removed).

points.label: Difference from UPI
points.text: Cards work offline in shops. UPI needs internet and both people to be in the system.

slides.inSimpleWords: A debit card is a plastic UPI card. It works everywhere—shops, ATMs, online.

image.alt: Debit Cards — Your Bank in Your Pocket — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Online Payments & E-Commerce
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to buy a book from an online store. He learns he can pay using UPI, debit card, or even a digital wallet stored on the website. The book shop is 500 km away, but the payment is instant.

points.label: E-commerce payment
points.text: Buying things online: the shop sends an invoice, you pay through UPI/card/wallet, goods are shipped.

points.label: Payment modes online
points.text: UPI, debit/credit card, net banking (login to your bank, pay from there), digital wallets (Google Pay, Paytm saved balance).

points.label: Why online?
points.text: Safe, no cash to carry, instant receipt, easy refunds, delivery to your door.

slides.inSimpleWords: Online shops are like market stalls that ship to you. You pay digitally, they deliver.

image.alt: Online Payments & E-Commerce — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Safety Rules for Digital Money
slides.storyContext: Mom gives Arjun critical advice: 'Digital money is safe, but you must be careful. Never share your PIN, password, or card details with anyone—not even friends.'

points.label: Your PIN is secret
points.text: Your PIN/password is like the key to your locker. Never tell anyone, not even friends or family.

points.label: Never share card/UPI details
points.text: Don't send your card number or UPI ID to unknown people. Use QR codes instead.

points.label: Use official apps
points.text: Only download Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm from Google Play Store or Apple App Store.

points.label: Check before sending
points.text: Always verify the receiver's name and amount before you hit 'Send'.

slides.inSimpleWords: Digital money is safe because banks track it. But you must guard your PIN like a dragon guards gold.

image.alt: Safety Rules for Digital Money — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Arjun's Real Transaction
slides.storyContext: Arjun buys a cricket bat for ₹2,500 at a sports shop using his debit card. Let's see what happens behind the scenes.

example.problem: Arjun goes to a shop with his debit card. The bat costs ₹2,500. He swipes his card. What happens?
example.solution:
Step 1: Arjun swipes his debit card at the shop's machine.
Step 2: The machine sends his card details to the bank securely.
Step 3: The bank checks Arjun's account balance (he has ₹5,000).
Step 4: The bank approves the transaction and sends a signal to the shop.
Step 5: The shop terminal prints a receipt showing ₹2,500 deducted.
Step 6: Arjun's bank account balance becomes ₹2,500 (5,000 - 2,500).
Step 7: He gets a text from the bank: 'Debit of ₹2,500 done at ShopName. Balance: ₹2,500.'
Step 8: The shop's account gets credited ₹2,500 after a day or two (settlement).
Key point: Money moved digitally, no cash touched, full record created.

image.alt: Arjun's Real Transaction — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Zara's Challenge to Arjun
slides.storyContext: Zara says: 'I owe you ₹200. I'll pay through UPI. But I also want to order books online for ₹800. My mom says I can only use her debit card at the shop (not online). What should I do?'

example.problem: Zara needs to: (1) send Arjun ₹200 via UPI, and (2) buy books worth ₹800 at an online store but only has a debit card for in-shop use. What are her options?
example.solution:
Option 1: For UPI payment to Arjun:
- Download Google Pay on her phone.
- Link her bank account and create a UPI ID (e.g., zara@upi).
- Send Arjun ₹200 instantly to his UPI ID.
- Arjun's money arrives in seconds. Done!

Option 2: For online book purchase:
- Go to the online shop and add books to the cart.
- Click 'Checkout' and choose 'Debit Card' as payment method.
- Enter her mom's card details (or her mom enters them).
- The card is charged ₹800; books are shipped to her address.

Alternative: Mom can use Google Pay to pay ₹800 for the books online. Her UPI is accepted at most online shops too.

Key learning: UPI is for person-to-person (peer-to-peer). Debit card works at online shops. Different tools for different jobs.

image.alt: Zara's Challenge to Arjun — Digital Money — UPI, Cards & Online Payments

slides.title: Arjun's First Mistake
slides.storyContext: One day, Arjun receives a text: 'Hi, your bank here. Please click here to update your account.' He almost clicks, but his mom stops him. 'That's a scam, beta. Real banks never ask for passwords by text. Let me show you the red flags.'

slides.title: Recognizing Digital Payment Scams

points.label: Phishing texts
points.text: Banks NEVER ask for passwords via SMS or email. If you get such a message, ignore it.

points.label: Fake apps
points.text: Download only from official Google Play Store or Apple App Store. Check ratings and reviews.

points.label: Too-good-to-be-true offers
points.text: If someone promises free money or massive discounts, it's a scam.

points.label: Unexpected payment requests
points.text: Don't send money to unknown people, even if they claim to be from your school or bank.

slides.inSimpleWords: If something feels suspicious in digital payment, stop and ask a trusted adult.

slides.title: Wallet vs. Bank Account — What's the Difference?

points.label: Digital wallet
points.text: A smaller pouch of money you carry on your phone (Google Pay, PhonePe). Limited amount, easy to spend.

points.label: Bank account
points.text: Your vault at the bank. Larger money, linked to a debit card. Interest may be earned.

points.label: Linked wallets
points.text: Your Google Pay wallet is connected to your bank account. It draws from there.

points.label: Best practice
points.text: Keep most money in your bank account. Use wallet for daily small purchases.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bank account is your main vault; wallet is your pocket money. Both are digital and safe.

slides.title: Arjun Learns About Transaction Limits
slides.storyContext: Arjun's mom tells him: 'Some payment methods have daily limits. You can't send infinite money in one day. This is for safety.' Let's see what this means.

example.problem: Arjun wants to send ₹1,000 to his friend via UPI in the morning, then ₹1,000 again in the afternoon. But his app says: 'Daily limit of ₹1,500 reached.' Why?
example.solution:
UPI and wallet apps have daily transaction limits:
- UPI limit: Usually ₹1,00,000 per day (varies by bank and app).
- But your BANK's daily transfer limit might be lower (e.g., ₹10,000 or ₹50,000).
- Arjun's limit is ₹1,500 per day, set by his bank.
- He's already sent ₹1,000, so only ₹500 remains.
- He must wait until midnight (next day) to send another ₹1,500.

Why limits?
1. Safety: Prevents large scams in one go.
2. Fraud protection: Banks monitor unusual activity.
3. Balance: Stops you from overspending.

Arjun can ask his mom or the bank to increase this limit if needed.

slides.title: QR Codes — The Safest Way to Pay

points.label: What is a QR code
points.text: A square barcode that stores payment information. Scan it to pay instead of typing.

points.label: How to scan
points.text: Open Google Pay or PhonePe, tap 'Scan,' point at the QR code. The receiver's details appear.

points.label: Why it's safer
points.text: You never type or speak the UPI ID, so no typos. Less chance of fraud.

points.label: Where you see them
points.text: At shops, restaurants, online invoices, even birthday cards. QR codes are everywhere.

slides.inSimpleWords: QR codes are like shortcuts. Scan instead of typing to pay faster and safer.

slides.title: Mom's Savings Tip
slides.storyContext: Mom opens the bank app and shows Arjun his savings account. 'Look, you've saved ₹2,000 already! And the bank paid you ₹50 as interest.' Arjun is confused. 'Interest? What's that?'

slides.title: Bank Interest — Your Money Earns More

points.label: What is interest
points.text: A reward the bank pays you for letting them keep your money. Like rent for your money.

points.label: How it's calculated
points.text: If you keep ₹1,000 for one year at 4% interest, you earn ₹40 extra (1000 × 0.04 = 40).

points.label: Compound interest
points.text: Interest on your interest! Year 2: You have ₹1,040, and it earns ₹41.60. It grows faster.

points.label: Why save?
points.text: More money over time. Good habit for the future.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks pay you to save. The longer you keep money there, the more it grows.

slides.title: Arjun's Savings Goal
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to buy a smartphone for ₹10,000 in one year. He saves ₹200 every month and gets 3% annual interest on his savings account.

example.problem: If Arjun saves ₹200/month for 12 months at 3% annual interest, will he have ₹10,000?
example.solution:
Savings over 12 months:
₹200 × 12 = ₹2,400 from savings alone.

But he also gets interest!
Average balance over the year ≈ ₹1,200 (grows from 0 to 2,400).
Interest earned ≈ ₹1,200 × 3% = ₹36.

Total after 1 year ≈ ₹2,400 + ₹36 = ₹2,436.

He needs ₹10,000 for the phone.
To reach this, he needs to:
1. Save more per month (maybe ₹700/month)?
2. Wait longer (maybe 5 years of saving + interest)?
3. Find another income source (part-time work)?

Learning: Interest helps, but small savings grow slowly. Plan ahead!

slides.title: Credit Cards vs. Debit Cards

points.label: Debit card
points.text: Spend money you HAVE now. Comes directly from your bank account.

points.label: Credit card
points.text: Borrow money and pay later. The card company lends you money; you get a bill at month-end.

points.label: For kids
points.text: Too young for credit cards. Debit cards and wallets are better. Credit is for adults.

points.label: Credit score
points.text: If you use credit cards responsibly (pay on time), you build a good credit score for loans later.

slides.inSimpleWords: Debit = spend your own money now. Credit = borrow and pay back later. Debit is safer for kids.

slides.title: Arjun's Money Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun gets two options: (1) Save ₹100/month for 10 years at 2% interest, or (2) Save ₹200/month for 5 years at 3% interest. Which gets him more money? Help him decide!

example.problem: Calculate total savings + interest for both plans. Which plan gives more money?
example.solution:
Plan 1: Save ₹100/month for 10 years at 2%
- Savings: ₹100 × 120 months = ₹12,000
- Rough interest: ₹12,000 × 2% × 5.5 years (average) = ₹1,320
- Total: ≈ ₹13,320

Plan 2: Save ₹200/month for 5 years at 3%
- Savings: ₹200 × 60 months = ₹12,000
- Rough interest: ₹12,000 × 3% × 2.5 years (average) = ₹900
- Total: ≈ ₹12,900

Both plans put in the same ₹12,000, but Plan 1 (longer time, lower rate) earns more interest because compound interest works over 10 years.

Key insight: Time is money. Saving earlier, even small amounts, beats saving more later!

slides.title: Arjun Goes Online Shopping
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to buy a book for ₹500 from an online store. His mom says, 'Let me teach you how to shop safely online and check if the website is real.'

slides.title: Safe Online Shopping Tips

points.label: Check the website
points.text: Look for 'https://' (not 'http://') and a padlock symbol. These mean the site is secure.

points.label: Verify the seller
points.text: Check reviews, ratings, and return policies. Known sites like Amazon, Flipkart are safer.

points.label: Read the invoice
points.text: Confirm the item, price, delivery address, and estimated arrival date before paying.

points.label: Payment method
points.text: Use UPI, debit card, or wallet on trusted platforms. Never send cash in advance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Online shopping is safe if you check the website and seller first.

slides.title: Tracking Orders and Returns

points.label: Order confirmation
points.text: After payment, you get an order ID and tracking number via email or SMS.

points.label: Tracking status
points.text: Log into the app/website and see if your order is 'Processing,' 'Shipped,' or 'Delivered.'

points.label: Delivery days
points.text: Most orders arrive in 2–7 days. Urgent/Premium options cost more but arrive faster.

points.label: If wrong item arrives
points.text: Contact customer service with your order ID. You can return it and get a refund or exchange.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every online order is tracked. If something goes wrong, you can return it easily.

slides.title: Arjun's Online Purchase Walkthrough
slides.storyContext: Arjun finds a book called 'Young Entrepreneurs Guide' on a trusted online store for ₹399. Let's walk through the purchase step-by-step.

example.problem: Arjun wants to buy a ₹399 book online using his debit card. Describe the entire process from searching to receiving.
example.solution:
Step 1: Search and Add to Cart
- Arjun searches for the book on Amazon/Flipkart.
- He clicks on the product, reads reviews (4.5 stars, 120 reviews).
- He adds it to his cart.

Step 2: Review and Checkout
- He views his cart: Book ₹399 + Delivery ₹0 (free) = Total ₹399.
- He confirms his delivery address (his home).
- He selects Debit Card as payment.

Step 3: Payment
- He enters his mom's debit card details (or she does).
- He enters the 4-digit PIN on the shop's secure payment page.
- Boom! Payment confirmed. He gets a receipt.

Step 4: Order Confirmation
- His mom receives an email with Order ID #12345.
- An SMS arrives: 'Your book has been shipped. Expected delivery: 3 days.'

Step 5: Tracking
- He logs into the app and sees: 'Shipped from warehouse on Day 1.'
- Day 2: 'Out for delivery.'
- Day 3: 'Delivered. Package left at your door.'

Step 6: Receive and Confirm
- Arjun receives the book in perfect condition.
- He clicks 'Confirm Delivery' in the app.
- His mom gets her money back immediately from temporary hold.

If the book was damaged?
- He'd click 'Report Issue' and start a return process.
- The seller would send a pickup person, and he'd get a refund in 5–7 days.

slides.title: Emergency: Payment System Down
slides.storyContext: One day, Arjun tries to pay for lunch at school, but his UPI app won't load. 'The internet is down,' says the teacher. 'What do you do now?' Arjun must think fast!

example.problem: You're at a shop, internet is down, UPI won't work. You have a debit card. Can you pay? What if you only have a wallet?
example.solution:
Scenario 1: You have a debit card
- Debit card transactions are possible OFFLINE using Chip and PIN.
- You can still swipe/tap the card; the machine stores data and uploads later when internet returns.
- Risk: Card details might be visible in offline mode (slightly higher risk than online).

Scenario 2: You only have a wallet
- Digital wallet requires internet; it won't work offline.
- Solution: Ask a friend to pay and return the favor when systems are back online.
- Carry some cash backup for emergencies like this.

Scenario 3: Real emergency backup
- Carry a small emergency cash pouch (₹200–500) for when digital systems fail.
- It's the smart thing to do, not going backward!

points.text: Digital money is real rupees that move through phones and banks, not cash.
UPI is the fastest way to send money person-to-person using a UPI ID (VPA).
Debit cards are linked to your bank account; swipe to pay anywhere.
Online shopping uses UPI, debit card, or net banking to pay; goods are shipped.
Always keep your PIN and card details secret.
Digital money is safer than cash because banks record every transaction.
Check amount and receiver before you send; it's instant and hard to reverse.
QR codes are the safest way to pay—scan instead of typing.
Recognize scams: Banks never ask for passwords via SMS. Download apps only from official stores.
Savings accounts earn interest—your money grows over time.
Online shopping is safe if you verify the website and seller first.
Track orders and easily return items if needed.
Have a backup: Debit cards work offline; wallets need internet. Carry emergency cash.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's Mystery Box
hook: Arun runs a juice stand at the Delhi fair and uses letters to price his drinks quickly.

slides.title: Arun's Mystery Box
slides.storyContext: A fair in Delhi. Arun sells fresh orange juice and wants to count bottles fast.

slides.title: The Problem
slides.storyContext: Every morning Arun starts with 5 bottles of juice already made. Throughout the day, he makes fresh batches. Priya asks: 'How many bottles will we have by evening if you make b batches of 4 bottles each?' Arun scratches his head. He needs a shorthand to track this quickly.
slides.inSimpleWords: When something changes (like batches made), we use a letter to stand for the unknown number so we don't have to keep guessing.

slides.title: What is an Expression?

points.text: An algebraic expression uses letters (called variables) to stand for unknown numbers.
Numbers we know are called constants.
We use letters like a, b, x, y to show quantities that change or we don't know yet.

example.problem: Arun starts with 5 bottles and makes b batches of 4 bottles each. Write an expression for total bottles.
example.solution: Total = 5 + 4b (the letter b is the variable; 5 and 4 are constants)

slides.inSimpleWords: An expression is a math sentence that has letters standing in for numbers.

slides.title: Terms in an Expression

points.text: Each part of an expression separated by + or − is called a term.
A term can be a single number, a single letter, or a number times a letter.
In 5 + 4b, the terms are 5 and 4b.

example.problem: Identify all terms in the expression 3x + 7 − 2y.
example.solution: The terms are: 3x, 7, and 2y (note: 2y is a term even though there is a minus sign)

slides.inSimpleWords: Terms are the building blocks of an expression — separate them by + and − signs.

image.alt: Terms in an Expression — Expressions using Letter-Numbers

slides.title: Coefficients

points.text: A coefficient is the number in front of a variable.
In 4b, the coefficient is 4 (it tells us how many groups of b we have).
If you see just b with no number, the coefficient is 1.

example.problem: In the expression 3x + 5y − 7, what are the coefficients of x and y?
example.solution: Coefficient of x is 3. Coefficient of y is 5. The 7 is a constant (no variable).

slides.inSimpleWords: The coefficient is the number stuck to the letter — it tells you how many of that variable.

slides.title: Writing Real Expressions

points.text: Listen to the story, identify what changes, and use a letter for it.
Example: Priya buys notebooks at ₹m each and pens at ₹6 each. If she buys 3 notebooks and 5 pens, the cost is 3m + 30.
The letter m changes (different notebooks cost different amounts), but 6 and 5 are fixed.

example.problem: At a market, apples cost ₹a per kg. Priya buys 2 kg of apples and 1 kg of guavas at ₹15. Write the total cost.
example.solution: Total cost = 2a + 15

slides.inSimpleWords: Real-life problems have unknown prices or quantities — use letters for those unknowns.

slides.title: Like and Unlike Terms

points.text: Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power. Example: 3x and 5x are like terms.
Unlike terms have different variables or different powers. Example: 3x and 3y are unlike.
We can add or subtract like terms; we cannot combine unlike terms.

example.problem: Combine like terms: 2a + 3a + 5b − b.
example.solution: 2a + 3a = 5a. And 5b − b = 4b. So the simplified expression is 5a + 4b.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only combine terms that have the exact same letter — they are like terms.

image.alt: Like and Unlike Terms — Expressions using Letter-Numbers

slides.title: Priya's Market Bill
slides.storyContext: Priya writes down what she bought: x mangoes at ₹12 each, y oranges at ₹8 each, and 1 coconut for ₹30.

example.problem: Write Priya's total bill as an expression. Then, if x = 3 and y = 5, find the total cost.
example.solution: Expression: 12x + 8y + 30. Substituting x = 3 and y = 5: 12(3) + 8(5) + 30 = 36 + 40 + 30 = ₹106.

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you know the values of the letters, substitute them in and calculate the total.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Arun's juice stand gets messy. He has 4 crates with j bottles in each, plus 2 loose bottles on the counter. Priya has 3 crates with j bottles in each, plus 1 loose bottle. How many bottles does each have?

example.problem: Write expressions for Arun's and Priya's bottle counts. If j = 10, who has more?
example.solution: Arun: 4j + 2. Priya: 3j + 1. If j = 10: Arun has 4(10) + 2 = 42. Priya has 3(10) + 1 = 31. Arun has more.

slides.inSimpleWords: Build the expression from the story, then plug in the number to find the real answer.

slides.title: Arun's Pricing Problem
slides.storyContext: Arun decides to create a price list for his juice stand. 'If I charge ₹p per small glass and ₹2p per large glass, and today I sold 20 small and 10 large glasses, how much did I earn? Let me use an expression to figure it out quickly.'

slides.title: Building Expressions from Word Problems

points.label: Step 1: Identify unknowns
points.text: What changes or isn't given? Assign a letter to it.

points.label: Step 2: Identify fixed values
points.text: What numbers are given and won't change?

points.label: Step 3: Translate words to math
points.text: 'Per' means multiply. 'Total' means add. 'Difference' means subtract.

points.label: Step 4: Write the expression
points.text: Combine the letter and numbers using +, −, ×.

example.problem: Arun's small glass sells for ₹p and large for ₹2p. He sold 20 small and 10 large today. Write an expression for total earnings.
example.solution:
Earnings from small: 20p
Earnings from large: 10 × 2p = 20p
Total: 20p + 20p = 40p

slides.inSimpleWords: Break down the word problem into pieces, then put them together as an expression.

slides.title: Substituting Values into Expressions

points.label: Replace the letter
points.text: When you know the value of a variable, write it in place of the letter.

points.label: Solve step-by-step
points.text: 3(2) + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11. Do multiplication/division first, then addition/subtraction.

points.label: Order of operations
points.text: BODMAS: Brackets, Orders, Division/Multiplication (left-to-right), Addition/Subtraction (left-to-right).

example.problem: If p = 30, find the total earnings from Arun's juice stand (40p).

slides.inSimpleWords: Substitution means replacing letters with numbers and calculating.

slides.title: Arun's Daily Earnings
slides.storyContext: If Arun charges ₹30 per small glass and ₹60 per large glass, and the expression for his earnings is 20p + 20p (where p = small glass price), how much did he earn today?

example.problem: Use the expression 40p to find Arun's earnings if p = 30.
example.solution:
Expression: 40p (from 20p + 20p)
Substituting p = 30:
40 × 30 = 1,200

Arun earned ₹1,200 today!

slides.title: Simplifying Complex Expressions

points.label: Combine like terms
points.text: 2x + 3x = 5x. Do this first.

points.label: Constants together
points.text: 7 + 5 = 12. Combine all standalone numbers.

points.label: Write in order
points.text: Variables first, then constants: 5x + 12 (not 12 + 5x, though both are correct).

points.label: Two variables
points.text: If you have 2x + 3y + 4x + 2y, combine: (2x + 4x) + (3y + 2y) = 6x + 5y.

example.problem: Simplify: 3a + 2b + 5a − b.
example.solution:
Combine like terms:
3a + 5a = 8a
2b − b = b
Simplified: 8a + b

slides.inSimpleWords: Simplify by grouping same variables and combining them.

slides.title: Priya's Inventory Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya helps Arun track juice bottles. She writes: 'We start with 50 bottles. Each day, we make d new bottles and sell s bottles. After 5 days, how many bottles are left?' She uses an expression to figure it out.

slides.title: Two-Variable Expressions

points.label: What are they
points.text: Expressions with more than one variable, like 50 + 5d − 5s.

points.label: Reading carefully
points.text: Each variable represents something different. d = daily production, s = daily sales.

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: Inventory tracking, profit calculations, distance-time problems all use two or more variables.

example.problem: Write an expression for bottles left after 5 days. If d = 12 and s = 10, how many remain?
example.solution:
Expression: 50 + 5d − 5s
Substituting d = 12, s = 10:
50 + 5(12) − 5(10) = 50 + 60 − 50 = 60 bottles

slides.inSimpleWords: Two variables mean two unknown quantities. Substitute both to find the answer.

slides.title: Priya's Weekly Inventory
slides.storyContext: Over one week, Arun's juice stand starts with 100 bottles. Each day Priya makes 15 new bottles, and the stand sells 18 bottles. She writes the expression: 100 + 7(15) − 7(18).

example.problem: How many bottles remain after 7 days?
example.solution:
Expression: 100 + 7(15) − 7(18)
Step 1: 7 × 15 = 105 bottles made
Step 2: 7 × 18 = 126 bottles sold
Step 3: 100 + 105 − 126 = 79 bottles

After one week, 79 bottles are in the stand.

slides.title: Can You Create This Expression?
slides.storyContext: Arun has a challenge for Priya: 'I start a week with w bottles. Each day I buy n new bottles and the stand sells 25 bottles. Write an expression for bottles left after 7 days. If w = 80 and n = 20, how many remain?'

example.problem: Create and solve the expression for Arun's challenge.
example.solution:
Expression: w + 7n − 7(25) = w + 7n − 175

Substituting w = 80, n = 20:
80 + 7(20) − 175 = 80 + 140 − 175 = 45 bottles

Arun has 45 bottles left after 7 days.

slides.title: Expression Patterns
slides.storyContext: Priya discovers something cool: 'Every 10 bottles we make, we earn extra profit. The pattern is 10k + 5, where k is groups of 10 bottles. Let's find the pattern!'

slides.title: Finding Patterns with Expressions

points.label: What is a pattern
points.text: A repeating rule or sequence that can be written as an expression.

points.label: Linear patterns
points.text: The simplest: 2n + 1 (double a number and add 1). Each value of n gives a different result.

points.label: Example sequence
points.text: For 2n + 1: if n = 1,2,3,4,5 then values are 3,5,7,9,11 (odd numbers!).

points.label: Using expressions
points.text: Instead of listing numbers, use one formula. Faster and more powerful.

example.problem: Find the pattern: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Write an expression using n.
example.solution:
The pattern multiplies: 5×1, 5×2, 5×3, 5×4, 5×5.
Expression: 5n (where n = 1,2,3,4,5,...)

slides.inSimpleWords: Expressions describe patterns using one formula instead of listing many numbers.

slides.title: Algebra and Money
slides.storyContext: One day, Priya says to Arun: Your drink prices and costs are perfect algebra problems.

slides.title: Variables in Business

points.text: Fixed cost: overhead like rent, stays constant.
Variable cost: depends on production quantity.
Revenue: price per unit times quantity sold.
Profit = Revenue minus (Fixed + Variable Costs).

slides.inSimpleWords: Businesses use expressions to track money flow.

slides.title: Arun Profit Calculation
slides.storyContext: Arun charges 20 per glass, fixed cost = 2000/day, variable = 8/glass.

example.problem: If he sells 300 glasses, what is profit?

slides.title: Breaking Even
slides.storyContext: When does Arun break even?

example.problem: Find n when profit = 0 using 12n - 2000 = 0
example.solution: 12n = 2000, n = 167 glasses to break even

slides.title: Equations vs Expressions

points.label: Expression
points.text: Math phrase: 3x + 5. No equal sign.

points.label: Equation
points.text: Equal statement: 3x + 5 = 20. Has equal sign.

points.label: Solving
points.text: Finding x value that makes equation true.

points.label: Use
points.text: Expressions show patterns. Equations answer what-if questions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expression is recipe; equation asks does it make the dish?

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Algebraic expressions use letters (variables) to represent unknown or changing quantities.
Terms are the parts of an expression separated by + or − signs.
A coefficient is the number in front of a variable.
Like terms have the same variable; unlike terms do not.
We can substitute known values into an expression to calculate a result.
Build expressions by translating real-world problems into math sentences.
Simplify by combining like terms and constants.
Two-variable expressions handle problems with multiple unknowns.
Order of operations (BODMAS) guides the order of calculations.
Expressions describe patterns more powerfully than listing numbers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expressions let us write math problems without knowing the exact numbers — we discover them later.

subject: Mathematics
chapter: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
title: Where the Roads Cross
hook: In Mumbai, two busy streets cross, and a third street nearby creates angles. Rohan must explain these angles for his school project.

characters.name: Uncle Dev
characters.role: auto-rickshaw driver, knows the city well

slides.title: Where the Roads Cross
slides.storyContext: Two main streets of Mumbai meet. Uncle Dev's auto-rickshaw navigates the intersection, and Rohan learns angles.

slides.title: The Intersection
slides.storyContext: Rohan is sitting in Uncle Dev's auto during rush hour. He notices that two roads cross perfectly, making four corners. Then a third road joins in from the side. 'Uncle, why are all these lines special?' Uncle Dev smiles. 'Geometry, beta. See how these roads create different angles? Let me teach you.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When two lines meet, they form angles. A third line crossing nearby creates even more angles to discover.

slides.title: Intersecting Lines

points.text: Two lines that cross each other at one point are called intersecting lines.
The point where they meet is the point of intersection.
Intersecting lines form four angles at their meeting point.

example.problem: Two roads cross at a traffic light in Delhi. Name the four angles formed.
example.solution: If the roads are line AB and line CD intersecting at O, the four angles are ∠AOC, ∠COB, ∠BOD, and ∠DOA.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two lines crossing make a point of intersection and create four angles around it.

slides.title: Vertically Opposite Angles

points.text: When two lines intersect, the angles opposite each other are equal.
These are called vertically opposite angles (or vertical angles).
If one angle is 60°, the angle directly opposite is also 60°.

example.problem: Two intersecting roads form an angle of 75°. What is the measure of the angle opposite to it?
example.solution: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the opposite angle is also 75°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles at an intersection are always equal — that's a property you can trust.

slides.title: Adjacent Angles

points.text: When two lines intersect, angles that share a side are called adjacent angles.
Adjacent angles formed by intersecting lines are supplementary (they add to 180°).
If one angle is 60°, the angle next to it is 180° − 60° = 120°.

example.problem: At a road crossing, two intersecting lines form angles. One angle is 110°. What is the measure of the adjacent angle?
example.solution: Adjacent angles sum to 180°. So 180° − 110° = 70°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles next to each other at an intersection always add up to 180° (a straight line).

slides.title: Parallel Lines and a Transversal

points.text: Parallel lines never intersect (they stay the same distance apart).
A line that crosses two parallel lines is called a transversal.
A transversal creates eight angles (four at each intersection point).

example.problem: Two railway tracks run parallel. A road crosses both. The road makes a 65° angle with the first track. What angle does it make with the second track?
example.solution: Corresponding angles are equal when a transversal crosses parallel lines. So the angle is also 65°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines are like railway tracks; a road crossing both makes the same angle at each track.

slides.title: Corresponding Angles

points.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, angles in the same position at each intersection are corresponding angles.
Corresponding angles are equal.
This is true only if the two lines are parallel.

example.problem: A street crosses two parallel lanes. The angle on the left of the transversal at the first lane is 70°. What is the corresponding angle at the second lane?
example.solution: Corresponding angles are equal, so it is 70°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matching angles at the two intersections are the same when the two lines are parallel.

slides.title: Rohan's Homework Problem
slides.storyContext: Rohan's teacher asks: 'Three roads meet at a crossing in a city. Road A and Road B intersect. Road C is parallel to Road B. Find all the angles if one angle at the A-B intersection is 50°.'

example.problem: Two lines intersect at one angle of 50°. A third line is parallel to one of them. List all angles formed.
example.solution: At the intersection of A and B: 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (opposite angles equal, adjacent sum to 180°). Where C (parallel to B) meets A: also 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (corresponding angles equal).

slides.inSimpleWords: Using angle properties, you can find all angles if you know just one.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev points out two roads in Mumbai. 'Beta, see these two roads? They cross. And that road over there is parallel to one of them. One angle at the crossing is 65°. Can you find all eight angles formed by the parallel road and the crossing road?'

example.problem: Two lines intersect at 65° (and its related angles). A third parallel line is cut by one of the original lines. Find all angles.
example.solution: At the original intersection: 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°. At the parallel line intersection: 65°, 115°, 65°, 115° (corresponding angles).

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw the lines, mark what you know, then use angle rules to find the rest.

slides.title: Rohan's Project Deepens
slides.storyContext: For his school project, Rohan discovers that roads don't just cross in simple patterns. Some roads make very acute (sharp) angles, others make obtuse (wide) angles. 'Uncle, what's the difference between 30° and 150°?'

slides.title: Types of Angles

points.label: Acute angle
points.text: Less than 90°. Sharp, pointy angle. Example: 45°, 60°, 30°.

points.label: Right angle
points.text: Exactly 90°. A perfect corner. Shown as a small square in diagrams.

points.label: Obtuse angle
points.text: Between 90° and 180°. Wide, open angle. Example: 120°, 150°, 135°.

points.label: Straight angle
points.text: Exactly 180°. A straight line. The widest possible angle.

example.problem: At a road crossing, identify each type of angle if one angle is 55°.
example.solution: 55° is acute. The adjacent angle is 180° − 55° = 125°, which is obtuse. Opposite to 55° is another 55° (acute). Opposite to 125° is another 125° (obtuse).

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles can be sharp (acute), perfect (right), wide (obtuse), or straight.

slides.title: Alternate Angles

points.label: What are they
points.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, alternate angles are on opposite sides of the transversal.

points.label: Alternate interior angles
points.text: On opposite sides, inside the parallel lines. They are equal.

points.label: Alternate exterior angles
points.text: On opposite sides, outside the parallel lines. They are also equal.

points.label: Different from corresponding
points.text: Corresponding angles are on the same side of the transversal. Alternate angles are on opposite sides.

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel railway tracks, creating an 80° angle on the left of the first track (inside). What is the alternate interior angle?
example.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal, so the angle on the right of the second track (inside) is also 80°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alternate angles are on opposite sides and are equal when the lines are parallel.

slides.title: Mumbai Traffic Intersection
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev points to a real intersection: two parallel streets with a diagonal road crossing both. 'Rohan, that diagonal is the transversal. Look at all the angles it makes!'

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel roads. The transversal makes a 58° angle with the first road. Identify all 8 angles at both intersections.
example.solution:
At the first intersection:
- Angle 1: 58°
- Angle 2 (adjacent): 180° − 58° = 122°
- Angle 3 (opposite to 1): 58°
- Angle 4 (opposite to 2): 122°

At the second intersection (parallel road):
- Angle 5 (corresponding to 1): 58°
- Angle 6 (corresponding to 2): 122°
- Angle 7 (corresponding to 3): 58°
- Angle 8 (corresponding to 4): 122°

Alternatively, using alternate angles:
- Angles 3 and 6 are alternate interior: both 58°
- Angles 2 and 5 are alternate interior: both 122°

slides.title: Co-Interior (Same-Side Interior) Angles

points.label: What are they
points.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, angles on the same side of the transversal and inside the lines are co-interior angles.

points.label: Key property
points.text: Co-interior angles are supplementary—they add to 180°.

points.label: Visual
points.text: Both angles are 'between' the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal.

points.label: Proof
points.text: If one co-interior angle is 70°, the other is 180° − 70° = 110°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One co-interior angle is 85°. What is the other?
example.solution: Co-interior angles sum to 180°. So 180° − 85° = 95°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Co-interior angles are on the same side, between the parallel lines, and they add to 180°.

slides.title: Rohan Tests His Knowledge
slides.storyContext: Rohan decides to test his new knowledge. He draws his own diagram of a street crossing and marks one angle as 72°. 'Can I find all other angles using what I learned?'

slides.title: Rohan's Complete Angle Diagram
slides.storyContext: Rohan draws two intersecting lines and marks one angle as 72°. Then he adds a parallel line with a transversal. He challenges himself to find all angles.

example.problem: Draw two intersecting lines. One angle is 72°. A third line is parallel to one of them, and a transversal cuts both lines. Find all angles at all intersections.
example.solution:
At the first intersection (original two lines):
- Angle A: 72° (given)
- Angle B (adjacent): 180° − 72° = 108°
- Angle C (opposite A): 72°
- Angle D (opposite B): 108°

At the parallel line (transversal with parallel line):
If the transversal makes 72° with the first line,
- Angle E (corresponding): 72°
- Angle F (adjacent): 108°
- Angle G (opposite E): 72°
- Angle H (opposite F): 108°

All angles at both intersections are either 72° or 108°.

slides.title: Real-World Application
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev says: 'In Mumbai, we have many parallel streets. If I know one angle at a street crossing, I can predict angles at every parallel street. That's geometry, beta!'

example.problem: Three parallel streets run north-south. Two transversals cross all three. The first transversal makes a 55° angle with the first street. What angles does it make with the other two streets? What about the second transversal if it makes 55° with the first street?
example.solution:
For the first transversal:
- Street 1: 55° (given) and 125° (supplementary)
- Street 2: 55° (corresponding) and 125° (supplementary)
- Street 3: 55° (corresponding) and 125° (supplementary)

For the second transversal:
- Street 1: 55° and 125°
- Street 2: 55° and 125°
- Street 3: 55° and 125°

Key insight: When a transversal crosses multiple parallel lines, it makes the same angles at every intersection.

slides.title: Rohan Discovers Angle Sum
slides.storyContext: While drawing more diagrams, Rohan notices: 'Wait, if I add up all four angles at an intersection, I always get 360°!' Let's explore this discovery.

slides.title: Angle Sum Around a Point

points.label: Full rotation
points.text: All angles around one point add up to 360° (a complete rotation).

points.label: At an intersection
points.text: Two intersecting lines create 4 angles: a° + b° + c° + d° = 360°.

points.label: Proof using known pairs
points.text: Opposite angles are equal (a=c, b=d). So a + b + a + b = 360, meaning 2a + 2b = 360, thus a + b = 180 (adjacent angles).

points.label: Straight line
points.text: A straight angle is exactly 180° (half the full rotation).

example.problem: Two intersecting lines form angles: 45°, x, 45°, x. Find x.
example.solution:
45 + x + 45 + x = 360
90 + 2x = 360
2x = 270
x = 135°

The angles are 45°, 135°, 45°, 135° (opposite angles are equal).

slides.inSimpleWords: All angles around a point sum to 360°—a complete circle.

slides.title: Reflex Angles

points.text: A reflex angle is between 180 and 360 degrees.
If regular angle is 60, reflex is 360 - 60 = 300.
Reflex angles rare in school but appear in 3D.
Example: spinning wheel can rotate short way or long way.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reflex angle is the long way around the circle.

slides.title: Rohan Draws a Complex Map
slides.storyContext: Rohan marks 3 parallel streets (NS) and 2 transversals crossing them.

slides.title: Angles with Multiple Transversals

points.text: Two transversals crossing parallel lines create patterns.
Each transversal creates same pattern at every parallel line.
Transversal A at 45 degrees: 45, 135, 45, 135 at each line.
Transversal B at 60 degrees: 60, 120, 60, 120 at each line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each transversal is independent, but follows same rules.

slides.title: Rohan Mumbai Map
slides.storyContext: Transversal A at 48 degrees, Transversal B at 62 degrees.

example.problem: List angles for both at first parallel street

slides.title: Perpendicular Lines

points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if they form 90 degree angle.
Symbol shows right angle.
At intersection: all four angles are 90 degrees.
Real-world: N-S streets perpendicular to E-W streets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular means at right angles, like a plus sign.

slides.title: Perpendicular Transversal
slides.storyContext: What if a transversal crosses parallel streets at 90 degrees?

example.problem: Transversal perpendicular to two parallel lines. List all angles.
example.solution: All angles: 90, 90, 90, 90 at every intersection

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Intersecting lines meet at a point and form four angles.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).
A transversal is a line crossing two other lines.
When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.
Alternate interior angles are equal (on opposite sides, inside parallel lines).
Co-interior angles sum to 180° (on same side, inside parallel lines).
Angles can be acute (sharp), right (90°), obtuse (wide), or straight (180°).
All angles around one point sum to 360°.
Real-world applications include street intersections, railway crossings, and architecture.

slides.inSimpleWords: Road crossings show us that angles follow rules: opposite angles match, and parallel lines with a crossing create matching angles.
